title: Two Planets Lighter Than Cotton Candy
hook: TOI-791 b and c are roughly Jupiter-sized but so bloated and gassy they'd float on water — and their unusually neat orbital rhythm is a rare clue to how puffed-up planets like this ever form.
key_points: TOI-791 b and c orbit a star 1,110 light-years away and are each about Jupiter's size but far lighter.
Their densities are 28-35x lower than Jupiter's — around 0.04 g/cm3, less dense than cotton candy.
The two planets lock into a 5:3 mean-motion resonance: the inner one orbits five times for every three of the outer one.
Only a handful of other known systems have more than one 'super-puff' planet, making this pairing rare.
Citizen scientists spotted the candidates in NASA TESS data; ground telescopes then confirmed them.
Their huge, light hydrogen-helium atmospheres likely puffed up while the planets formed farther from their star.
content_html: Not every giant planet is dense like Jupiter. TOI-791 b and c, orbiting a star about 1,110 light-years away, are each roughly Jupiter's size but carry a fraction of its mass — their densities work out to somewhere between 28 and 35 times lower than Jupiter's, around 0.04 grams per cubic centimeter. For comparison, cotton candy runs about 0.05 g/cm3: these planets are, by that measure, lighter than spun sugar.
extra_html: According to ScienceDaily, the pair was first flagged by citizen scientists combing through NASA's TESS survey data, then confirmed with ground-based follow-up including Antarctica's ASTEP telescope. What makes the system especially valuable to astronomers is the neat 5:3 mean-motion resonance between the two planets — the inner one completes five orbits for every three the outer one makes. Systems with more than one such "super-puff" are rare; only a handful are known. Researchers think planets like these built their oversized, gassy envelopes while still forming farther from their star, in a colder part of the system, and studying pairs locked in stable resonances like this one offers a rare, clean test of that idea.

related.title: Why Some Giant Planets Spin Faster Than 'Failed Stars'
related.hook: Astronomers clocked the spins of dozens of distant worlds and found a surprise: lightweight giant planets can twirl faster than the much heavier brown dwarfs — so mass isn't the whole story.

related.title: An Alien World With Two Different Twilights
related.hook: On a scorching giant planet that never turns away from its star, the James Webb telescope found that dawn and dusk look nothing alike — winds smear the heat from one side to the other.

flashcards.prompt: Why are TOI-791 b and c called 'super-puff' planets?
flashcards.back_html: They're roughly Jupiter's size but only about 1/30th as dense — around 0.04 g/cm3, less dense than cotton candy — because of their huge, lightweight hydrogen-helium atmospheres.

flashcards.prompt: What makes this particular pair of super-puffs unusually rare?

choices.text: They share a tight 5:3 mean-motion orbital resonance
They are the only super-puff planets ever found

flashcards.explanation_html: Multi-planet super-puff systems are already uncommon — only a few are known — and this pair's clean 5:3 resonance (five inner orbits per three outer orbits) makes it stand out.

flashcards.prompt: What does the planets' puffiness suggest about how they formed?
flashcards.back_html: They likely built up enormous hydrogen-helium atmospheres while forming farther from their star, in a colder region — a clue researchers use to reconstruct how such low-density giants come to exist.
